The store keeps only the event types in

through that conformance in CBOR (RFC 8949), a compact binary encoding, as a map of its properties

The log is a directory of append-only segment files: in Application Support on Apple platforms
(excluded from backups), and in the XDG state directory on Linux, unless
says
otherwise. Each segment starts with a magic number and format version. Each record, a CBOR map of
its identifier, timestamp, event name and schema version, call site and event, is framed by its
length and CRC-32. A segment is deleted once every record in it has been delivered, so a log with
nothing left to send holds no files.
The log never holds more than its byte bound, 5 MiB unless
says otherwise. When a
record won’t fit, the oldest segments are dropped, and each drop is reported on the store’s
with the number of records dropped and their timestamp range. So is a record whose
write to disk fails, which is kept in memory only. Recovery cuts a segment at its first torn or
corrupt record, keeps every record before it, and reports what it cut.
A record whose delivery had started when the app ended comes back with

An event’s type can change while records of it are still on disk, because each property is found
by its name: an app update reads the records the release before it left. A property removed since
is skipped, an optional property added since reads as
, one with a default value added since
reads as its default, and properties can be reordered. Those changes keep the event’s
, which is 1 unless the event says otherwise.
A change the earlier records can’t be read through raises the version: a property’s type changed,
a required property added without a default, an optional property made required. A record stored
at a different version from its type’s current one is dropped without being read, and reported on
with the event and both versions. A record without a version has none to compare and
is read by name. A record that can’t be read at the same version, after such a change made without
a new version, is dropped and reported as undecodable. Neither is ever delivered with a made-up
value, and records are never migrated from one version to another.

abstract.text: Tell the people and services that read your events what each event holds, and hear about a change that would break their data before it ships.
Keep a seeded fraction of the events a tracker tracks, event by event or a whole session at once.
Track screen views, control activations and the app’s lifecycle without a call at each place they happen.
Stamp every event with its session and with the app, device, system, locale and network it was tracked on.
Deliver an event only once the user grants the purpose it is collected for.
Keep each record on disk until it is delivered, so the records a tracker tracked survive the app ending.
An event’s version counts the changes that records stored before them can’t be read through, and only those. A compatible change keeps the version; a breaking one raises it.
Derive an event’s conformances and schema from its declaration with
, and constrain which values its properties may hold.
Typed analytics events for Swift, delivered in batches to any number of destinations.
Keep each record in a table of the app’s own GRDB database until it is delivered.
